"title": "Comparative Performance Analysis of Image De-noising Techniques",
"authors": "Vivek Kumar, Pranay Yadav, Atul Samadhiya, Sandeep Jain, and Prayag Tiwari",
"field_subfield": "Image Processing / Signal Processing",
"type_of_paper": "Survey / Review with comparative experimental study",
"executive_summary": "This paper provides a comprehensive account of image noise types and a comparative analysis of denoising algorithms, grounded in a single experimental evaluation on the Lena image. The authors argue that noise degrades image quality and appearance, and that selecting an appropriate denoising algorithm is application-dependent, requiring knowledge of the noise type present. They classify noise into additive (Gaussian, salt-and-pepper) and multiplicative (speckle) categories, and describe Brownian (1/f) noise as a fractal case. The paper then presents a detailed classification of denoising approaches into spatial filtering (linear and non-linear) and transform-domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet-based), with emphasis on thresholding methods (hard, soft, semi-soft, Garrote) and adaptive versus non-adaptive thresholds. Performance is evaluated using PSNR and IEF on a grayscale Lena image with 90% noise density. Results show that mean filter (6.5759 PSNR) and adaptive median filter (8.0603 PSNR) perform poorly, while MDBUTMF achieves the best performance at 17.9865 PSNR and 16.2066 IEF, outperforming MDBA (17.2242 PSNR) and DBA (17.1205 PSNR). The authors conclude that wavelet-based methods, particularly MDBUTMF, are promising, and suggest future research directions. The paper is primarily a survey with a limited comparative experiment, lacking detailed methodology, hardware specifications, and extensive ablations. It serves as a foundational reference for understanding noise types and denoising classifications, though its experimental scope is narrow and its quantitative claims are limited to a single image and noise density.",

summary.executive_summary: This paper provides a comprehensive account of image noise types and a comparative analysis of denoising algorithms, grounded in a single experimental evaluation on the Lena image. The authors argue that noise degrades image quality and appearance, and that selecting an appropriate denoising algorithm is application-dependent, requiring knowledge of the noise type present. They classify noise into additive (Gaussian, salt-and-pepper) and multiplicative (speckle) categories, and describe Brownian (1/f) noise as a fractal case. The paper then presents a detailed classification of denoising approaches into spatial filtering (linear and non-linear) and transform-domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet-based), with emphasis on thresholding methods (hard, soft, semi-soft, Garrote) and adaptive versus non-adaptive thresholds. Performance is evaluated using PSNR and IEF on a grayscale Lena image with 90% noise density. Results show that mean filter (6.5759 PSNR) and adaptive median filter (8.0603 PSNR) perform poorly, while MDBUTMF achieves the best performance at 17.9865 PSNR and 16.2066 IEF, outperforming MDBA (17.2242 PSNR) and DBA (17.1205 PSNR). The authors conclude that wavelet-based methods, particularly MDBUTMF, are promising, and suggest future research directions. The paper is primarily a survey with a limited comparative experiment, lacking detailed methodology, hardware specifications, and extensive ablations. It serves as a foundational reference for understanding noise types and denoising classifications, though its experimental scope is narrow and its quantitative claims are limited to a single image and noise density.

claims.description: Wavelet-based denoising methods, particularly MDBUTMF, outperform other filters in terms of PSNR and IEF.
Spatial filters, particularly mean and adaptive median filters, perform poorly compared to wavelet-based methods.

Executive Summary
This paper provides a comprehensive account of image noise types and a comparative analysis of denoising algorithms, grounded in a single experimental evaluation on the Lena image. The authors argue that noise degrades image quality and appearance, and that selecting an appropriate denoising algorithm is application-dependent, requiring knowledge of the noise type present. They classify noise into additive (Gaussian, salt-and-pepper) and multiplicative (speckle) categories, and describe Brownian (1/f) noise as a fractal case. The paper then presents a detailed classification of denoising approaches into spatial filtering (linear and non-linear) and transform-domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet-based), with emphasis on thresholding methods (hard, soft, semi-soft, Garrote) and adaptive versus non-adaptive thresholds. Performance is evaluated using PSNR and IEF on a grayscale Lena image with 90% noise density. Results show that mean filter (6.5759 PSNR) and adaptive median filter (8.0603 PSNR) perform poorly, while MDBUTMF achieves the best performance at 17.9865 PSNR and 16.2066 IEF, outperforming MDBA (17.2242 PSNR) and DBA (17.1205 PSNR). The authors conclude that wavelet-based methods, particularly MDBUTMF, are promising, and suggest future research directions. The paper is primarily a survey with a limited comparative experiment, lacking detailed methodology, hardware specifications, and extensive ablations. It serves as a foundational reference for understanding noise types and denoising classifications, though its experimental scope is narrow and its quantitative claims are limited to a single image and noise density.

Research Context
Image restoration aims to remove degradations such as blurring and noise. Noise is an important factor that reduces image quality and appearance. Selection of the denoising algorithm is application dependent. Knowledge about the noise present is necessary to select the appropriate algorithm. Different types of noises exist that corrupt images. Prior work has developed various denoising algorithms with trade-offs.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper aims to present a brief account on types of noises and their removal algorithms. The authors discuss noise types based on additive and multiplicative nature. The paper presents a precise classification and analysis of denoising algorithms. A comparative study of algorithms is conducted in context of performance evaluation. The authors conclude with several promising directions for future research.

Methodological Details
The study is a comparative analysis of image denoising techniques. The paper was published at ICIET 2013 in Bangkok, Thailand. The authors are Vivek Kumar, Pranay Yadav, Atul Samadhiya, Sandeep Jain, and Prayag Tiwari. The experiment used a grayscale image of Lena with 90% noise density. Performance was measured using PSNR and image enhancement factor (IEF). MSE stands for mean square error in the performance measures. IEF stands for image enhancement factor. M x N denotes the size of the image in the formulas. Y represents the original image in the notation. The de-noised image is denoted by a specific symbol. The noisy image is represented by the symbol η. The Lena image was used for the comparative study. The comparison is presented in Table I.

Procedures And Architectures
Two basic approaches of image denoising are identified. The approaches are spatial filtering and transform domain filtering. Spatial filters can be classified into non-linear and linear filters. Non-linear filters remove noise without explicitly identifying it. Spatial filters employ low pass filtering on groups of pixels. A mean filter is the optimal linear filter for Gaussian noise. Wiener filtering requires information about noise and signal spectra. Wiener filtering works well only if the underlying signal is smooth. Spatial-frequency filtering uses low pass filters with FFT. Wavelet domain filtering can be subdivided into linear and nonlinear methods. Hard thresholding removes small coefficients while leaving others untouched. Soft thresholding shrinks coefficients above the threshold. VISU Shrink is a non-adaptive universal threshold. SURE Shrink uses a hybrid of universal and SURE thresholds. Bayes Shrink minimizes the Bayes Risk Estimator function. Cross Validation replaces wavelet coefficient with weighted average. UDWT is shift invariant and avoids visual artifacts. Multiwavelets enhance performance but increase computation complexity. The deterministic method creates a tree structure of wavelet coefficients. Statistical modeling focuses on multi-scale and local correlation.

Key Results
The mean filter achieved the lowest PSNR among all filters. The mean filter achieved an IEF of 1.1712. The adaptive median filter achieved a PSNR of 8.0603. The adaptive median filter achieved an IEF of 1.6499. The PSMF filter achieved a PSNR of 6.7847. The PSMF filter achieved an IEF of 1.2257. The DBA filter achieved a PSNR of 17.1205. The DBA filter achieved an IEF of 13.2768. The MDBA filter achieved a PSNR of 17.2242. The MDBA filter achieved an IEF of 13.5976. The MDBUTMF filter achieved the best PSNR of 17.9865. The MDBUTMF filter achieved the best IEF of 16.2066. MDBUTMF outperformed MDBA by 0.7617 PSNR absolute. MDBUTMF outperformed DBA by 0.866 PSNR absolute. MDBUTMF outperformed MDBA by 4.47% relative PSNR. MDBUTMF outperformed DBA by 5.06% relative PSNR. MDBUTMF outperformed MDBA by 19.17% relative IEF. MDBUTMF outperformed DBA by 21.97% relative IEF. The results are presented in Table I. The study was conducted at 90% noise density. The results are limited to a single image and noise density.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The shift invariance of UDWT avoids visual artifacts. Multiwavelets enhance performance but increase computation complexity. The best performance was achieved at 90% noise density. The paper implies future research directions. The results are limited to a single image and noise density. The paper suggests noise type knowledge is important for algorithm selection. The study implies wavelet-based methods are promising for future research.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is limited to a single image (Lena) and noise density (90%). The results are limited to grayscale images. The paper omits detailed performance measures beyond PSNR and IEF. The study is primarily a survey with a limited comparative experiment.

Claims
Wavelet-based denoising methods, particularly MDBUTMF, outperform other filters in terms of PSNR and IEF. MDBUTMF achieved the best PSNR of 17.9865. MDBUTMF achieved the best IEF of 16.2066. MDBUTMF outperformed MDBA by 0.7617 PSNR absolute. MDBUTMF outperformed DBA by 0.866 PSNR absolute. The results are presented in Table I. The results are limited to a single image and noise density. Wavelet-based methods are promising for future research. The results suggest noise type knowledge is important for algorithm selection. The study implies future research directions.
Spatial filters, particularly mean and adaptive median filters, perform poorly compared to wavelet-based methods. The mean filter achieved the lowest PSNR of 6.5759. The adaptive median filter achieved a PSNR of 8.0603. The PSMF filter achieved a PSNR of 6.7847. The results are presented in Table I. The results are limited to a single image and noise density. The results suggest spatial filters are less effective. The study implies future research directions.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study is limited to a single image and noise density.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the Gaussian distribution. Figure 2 illustrates Gaussian noise with different parameters. Figure 3 shows the probability density function for salt and pepper noise. Figure 4 illustrates salt and pepper noise. Figure 5 shows the gamma distribution. Figure 6 illustrates speckle noise. Figure 7 shows the Brownian noise distribution. Figure 8 illustrates Brownian noise. Figure 9 shows the expanded classification of image denoising technique. Table I compares image parameters for different denoising filters. Table I shows MDBUTMF achieved the best PSNR of 17.9865. Table I shows MDBUTMF achieved the best IEF of 16.2066.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a comprehensive classification of image noise types and denoising algorithms. 2. The strongest evidence is that MDBUTMF achieved the best PSNR of 17.9865 and IEF of 16.2066. 3. The future path is to explore wavelet-based methods and their applications in various domains.
